She had been swimming at the club for about a year and a half and I had never once seen her race, because the races are on Saturday mornings and Saturday mornings were the plant. That autumn I told her I would be there, and then a client called on the Friday night about a delivery that had gone wrong, and I spent three hours on the phone and got to the pool forty minutes late. She had already swum. I stood at the side with the other parents watching a race she was not in, and one of them told me she had finished second, and had looked round at the wall for about ten seconds before the next race started. I had missed it by less than an hour. What I remember is not guilt exactly, it is that I had believed, right up until that morning, that these things averaged out. They do not average out. Each one is the only one of itself. I have not missed one since, and the deliveries have all somehow still happened.

The question we get asked is how to build a habit, and it is the wrong question, because most of the people asking already have several. They have been getting up at the same time for a decade. What they want to know, although they do not put it this way, is how to stop a good one from being taken. And the finding there is unglamorous. Habits that survive are the ones attached to a fixed point in the day that somebody else does not control, and habits that die are the ones that live in the space left over. If you exercise when the day allows it, you will exercise in quiet months and not in busy ones, which is precisely backwards, because the busy month is the one where it was doing something. We interviewed people two years after a big change at work. Almost everybody who had kept a routine had moved it earlier rather than protecting it where it was. They had not become more disciplined. They had simply put it somewhere nobody else could reach.

We travel in the off-season, because it is the only window that is ours.
